title: Capturing dynamics with noisy quantum computers
abstract_summary: This thesis (Chapter 2) analyzes approximation and generalization properties of parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs). It proves that, with simple input rescaling, PQCs can uniformly approximate functions in Lp, C0 and Sobolev Hk spaces, and derives generalization bounds that relate discretized Sobolev-type loss functions (including derivative information) to target distances such as Lp and supremum norms. The work explains why differential machine learning losses can improve generalization for PQC models and illustrates the results with numerical experiments.
methodology_description: The chapter develops a theoretical and numerical study of the approximation and generalization capacities of parameterized quantum circuits (PQC). Theoretical methodology: PQCs are modeled as expectation values f_theta(x)=<0|U^†(x;theta) M U(x;theta)|0> and expressed as generalized trigonometric series. The authors define a universal Hamiltonian family (tensor-product Pauli Hamiltonians as an example) and prove universality/approximation theorems in multiple function spaces (Lp for 1<=p<infty, C0 on compact subsets, and Sobolev H^k) by connecting PQC representable truncated Fourier/Fejér means to classical Fejér/Cèsaro summation theorems and Sobolev extension theorems. They derive generalization bounds relating discrete empirical losses that include derivative terms (DML / discretized H^k losses) to continuous target distances (L^p, C^0, H^k) using Rademacher complexity, Talagrand's lemma, and compact Sobolev embeddings (Rellich–Kondrachov). Practical recommendations (methodological prescriptions) include min–max feature scaling of inputs to the interval [-π/2, π/2]^N so PQCs can approximate in the stronger senses. Numerical methodology: small-scale numerical simulations illustrate theory. A layered PQC architecture with data-encoding Rx(omega x) rotations and variational Ry(theta) rotations per qubit is trained (Pauli-Z measurements) to approximate a 1D synthetic target function. Training experiments compare loss choices (mean-squared ℓ_{l2} vs. derivative-inclusive ℓ_{h1}) and different input normalizations, using the Adam classical optimizer, multiple trials, and plotting percentile bands to illustrate bias/variance and boundary/Gibbs-like effects.
algorithms_used: Data-reuploading / repeated data-encoding via Rx(omega * x)
experimental_setup: Classical simulation of PQC experiments (simulator/software unspecified). Architecture: layered PQC with per-qubit Rx(omega * x) data-encoding gates and Ry(theta) variational gates; measurements in Pauli-Z basis. Experiments used 10 training sample points (plus derivative values when applicable), training repeated 100 times, 100 epochs of Adam optimizer per run. Loss functions compared: empirical l2 (mean squared) and h1 (sum of MSE on function values and first derivatives). Input normalization variants tested: min-max scaling to [-π/2, π/2], [-π, π], and [-2π, 2π].

key_findings: [speculative] Parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) can be expressed as generalized trigonometric series whose accessible frequency spectrum is determined by the data-encoding Hamiltonian and whose coefficients are controlled by trainable gates.
[speculative] For a suitable ("universal") family of encoding Hamiltonians, PQC model families are universal approximators in Lp([0,2π]^N) for all 1 ≤ p < ∞ (Theorem 2.2).

[speculative] For functions continuous on a domain U compactly contained in [0,2π]^N, PQCs (with the stated encoding assumptions) can approximate the function uniformly (C0 convergence) to arbitrary precision (Theorem 2.3).

[speculative] PQCs can approximate target functions in Sobolev spaces H^k (i.e., approximating function values and derivatives up to order k) under the same encoding/universality conditions (Theorem 2.4).

[speculative] A simple min–max feature scaling (per-dimension linear map) that maps input features into the interval [−π/2, π/2]^N improves PQC expressivity and enables the above approximation results in practice (recommended normalization strategy).

[speculative] New generalization bounds are derived that relate empirical losses based on derivatives (discretized Sobolev losses Dh_k) to continuous target distances (Lp, Hk, and C0) for PQC model classes built from truncated trigonometric series (Theorems 2.5–2.7).

[speculative] In particular, minimizing the empirical Dh_k loss (sum of squared errors of function values and derivatives up to order k) yields control over the C0 (supremum) norm in the regime k > N/2 (uniform convergence), via compact embeddings (Rellich–Kondrachov).

[speculative] Theoretical results explain why differential machine learning (DML) losses that include derivative terms (ℓ_hk) can be consistent with stronger target metrics (e.g., C0) and thus can lead to better approximations for some problems.

[supported] Numerical simulations (1D experiments approximating the linear function f*(x)=x/2π with a small PQC) show that: (a) normalizing inputs to [−π/2, π/2] gives markedly better approximation than larger input ranges, (b) using the ℓ_h1 loss reduces variance and can reduce bias under the appropriate normalization, and (c) using ℓ_h1 under an inappropriate normalization (e.g., [−π,π]) can worsen approximation of function values because the model balances function and derivative errors.

[speculative] The discretized Sobolev (ℓ_hk) empirical loss requires more data and more circuit evaluations (scales with the number of derivatives), implying a practical curse-of-dimensionality for high input dimension and high k (exponential growth in mixed derivatives).
[supported] The work cites and connects to earlier empirical DML successes (e.g., prior 7D Basket option example) to motivate that derivative-based losses can be helpful in practice.
results_summary: This chapter develops a theoretical and partly empirical analysis of the approximation and generalization capacities of parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs). Building on prior work that represents PQC expectation values as generalized trigonometric series, the authors prove that, for suitable ("universal") encoding Hamiltonians, PQCs can approximate functions in Lp (1 ≤ p < ∞), uniformly approximate continuous functions on compact subsets (C0), and approximate functions in Sobolev spaces H^k (including derivatives) to arbitrary precision. They show that a practical per-dimension min–max scaling of inputs to [−π/2, π/2] is effective to meet the domain assumptions of the theorems. The chapter also derives new generalization bounds linking empirical discretized Sobolev losses (which include derivative information) to target distances (Lp, Hk, C0), giving a theoretical rationale for differential machine learning (DML) losses. Small-scale numerical simulations in 1D corroborate that proper normalization and derivative-aware losses can improve approximation quality, while improper normalization can harm it; the authors note practical costs (data and circuit evaluations) and dimensionality limitations for derivative-based losses.
quantum_advantage_detail: The chapter focuses on theoretical approximation and generalization properties of PQCs and on loss/normalization strategies; it does not claim or demonstrate a computational or scaling advantage of quantum models over classical methods.
